title: Where do evil and suffering come from?
summary: If God is good and almighty, where does evil come from? The Bible answers not with philosophy, but with the story of the great controversy: a world created good, love that requires freedom, rebellion in heaven, the fall of humanity - and a God who is not the author of evil, but the One who resolves it on the cross.

sections.heading: A world that came good from God's hands

items.comment: The original world was not a "mixture of good and evil". God assessed the whole creation as "very good" - evil did not belong to the original design.

questions.text: Since the world began as "very good", what does it tell us that today it does not look that way?

items.label: "very good" (Gen 1:31)
items.content: In Gen 1 the word "good" (Hebrew *tow*) returns like a refrain - six times during the act of creation, and at the end the climax: "very good" (*tow me'od*). It is not only an aesthetic judgment, but a testimony that the whole was in keeping with the design and free of evil. Evil is not an "unfinished detail" of the world, but a later intruder.

items.comment: "God is light, and in him there is no darkness at all." Evil cannot be laid on God - he is not its source.

questions.text: What changes in the picture of God when you are convinced that there is no "dark side" in him?

items.label: this is not an eternal dualism of good and evil
items.content: The biblical picture differs from dualism (for example, Persian or Gnostic), in which good and evil are two eternal, equal forces. Here evil is not an eternal counter-god: it appeared in time, within a created good that became corrupted - and that is why it can have an end. Light is original; darkness is its absence, not an eternal rival.

items.comment: God "is love". And love, by definition, cannot be forced - this is the key to understanding why the possibility of evil existed at all.

questions.text: Why would love that was programmed or compelled not be love at all?

items.comment: God sets before the human being a real choice: life or death - and says "choose". Freedom of choice is a gift, but it carries risk.

questions.text: Why must a genuine relationship allow for the possibility of saying "no"?

items.comment: "Choose this day whom you will serve." God never forces us to himself - he invites. The same risk that gives rise to love also allows for rebellion.

questions.text: What does it say about God that he prefers the risk of free love to the certainty of compelled obedience?

items.label: what the great controversy is about
items.content: The conflict is not about "who is stronger", but about the character of God, his law and his rule over the universe. Satan charges that God's government is unjust and that obedience out of love is impossible. That is why God does not end the conflict by force right away: he allows evil to expose itself before the whole universe, instead of "decreeing" his case.

questions.text: Why does a conflict "about the character of God" require time and evidence, rather than simply a verdict by force?

items.comment: God "stands at the door and knocks" - he waits for us to open from the inside. He never forces the door of the human heart.

questions.text: How does it change the picture of God that he knocks instead of entering by force?

sections.heading: The rebellion that began in heaven

items.comment: Evil has its origin in a real rebellion: "war in heaven", and Satan (a former angel) is cast down. Behind evil stands a person, not an abstraction.

questions.text: What changes when you realize that behind human struggles there is a larger conflict of which we are a part?

items.comment: Beneath the image of the fallen king of Babylon a deeper fall shows through: a fivefold "I will ascend... I will be like the Most High". The root of rebellion is pride and the desire to take God's place.

questions.text: How does "I want to be like God / in place of God" still tend, today, to be the root of evil in the human heart as well?

items.label: where the name "Lucifer" came from (Isa 14:12)
items.content: The Hebrew *helel ben-szachar* means "shining one, son of the dawn" (the morning star). The Latin Vulgate rendered it with the word *Lucifer* - "light-bearer". Hence the name "Lucifer" in tradition for the being behind the rebellion. The text itself shows a tragic irony: someone created to reflect light desired to take the place of the Source of light.

items.comment: Behind "the king of Tyre" one can see a being created "perfect", in whom "iniquity was found". Evil is not eternal - it appeared in someone good who chose it.

questions.text: What does it mean that evil did not exist "from forever", but arose in the heart of a being that was originally good?

items.label: the double perspective of Isa 14 and Ezek 28
items.content: Isa 14 (the king of Babylon) and Ezek 28 (the king of Tyre) are, on the surface, speeches against earthly rulers. At the same time the language of these texts (a being "perfect from the day of its creation", a presence "on God's holy mountain", a desire for equality with the Most High) exceeds what is possible for a human being, and it has traditionally been read as an unveiling of the power behind the pride of these kings. It is worth keeping both levels - the historical and the trans-historical - without losing either.

items.label: a cherub created sinless (Ezek 28:15)
items.content: The text says plainly: "you were perfect in your ways from the day you were created, until iniquity was found in you". This is crucial for understanding the origin of evil: it was not created by God, nor did it exist eternally - it arose in a being that was originally good, as an abuse of freedom. Evil is a "parasite" on good, not a separate material.

items.comment: Jesus calls the devil "the father of lies" and "a murderer from the beginning". The first weapon of rebellion is a distorted picture of God - a lie about his character.

questions.text: Which "lies about God" (that he is harsh, distant, unkind) are easiest to sow in us today?

items.label: "Satan" and "devil": accuser and slanderer
items.content: The Hebrew *satan* means "adversary, accuser" (the role of the accuser in a court, for example Job 1-2; Zech 3:1). The Greek *diabolos* is "slanderer, one who casts false accusations". Both names reveal the strategy: not so much force as lies and accusation - of God before humanity and of humanity before God. That is why it is good news that we have a Defender.

sections.heading: The fall of humanity and the great controversy as the frame of history

items.comment: The serpent does not begin with a command, but with a question that undermines God's word and goodness: "Did God really say...". The fall is, above all, the loss of trust.

questions.text: What really "broke" in the human being first: obedience, or trust in God's goodness?

items.comment: Already at the moment of the fall comes the first promise: "the offspring of the woman" will crush the head of the serpent. The great controversy has its resolution announced in advance.

questions.text: What does it mean to you that hope appears in exactly the place where evil appeared?

items.label: Gen 3:15 as the "protoevangelium"
items.content: This verse is sometimes called the *protoevangelium* - the "first Gospel". It is the earliest announcement in the Bible that the offspring of the woman will defeat the serpent, though he himself will be wounded ("he will crush your head, and you will wound his heel"). The whole subsequent history of salvation is an unfolding of this single promise given right after the fall.

items.comment: Through one man sin and death entered the world. Suffering and death are the consequence of separation from the Giver of life, not God's original design.

questions.text: How does it change your view of suffering to realize that it is an "intruder", and not something God planned?

items.label: the great controversy as the frame of the whole Bible
items.content: The biblical answer to evil is not philosophical, but narrative: the whole of history plays out as a conflict between Christ and Satan - a dispute over whether God is just and full of love. The bookends span Gen 3 (the lie sown) and Rev 20-22 (the final cleansing). This perspective binds individual texts into one story and explains why God tolerates evil for a time.

items.comment: The book of Job lifts the curtain: the suffering of a righteous man does not come from God, but from the accuser. It is God who is accused - not the author of the misfortune.

questions.text: How does it change the question "why did God do this to me" to realize that behind Job's suffering stands Satan, not God?

items.label: the heavenly "court" in the book of Job
items.content: Job 1-2 shows a scene in which the "sons of God" (heavenly beings) stand before God, and among them the accuser appears. It is a rare look "behind the scenes": human suffering is set within an ongoing dispute, where what is at stake is whether a person serves God out of love or only for gain. The reader knows what Job does not - which is why his suffering must not be read as punishment from God.

items.comment: The conflict continues to this day: the dragon "became furious" and wages war against those who hold to God. Our struggles have meaning within this larger story.

questions.text: What does it give you to realize that your personal battles are not random, but part of an ongoing conflict?

sections.heading: Suffering is temporary, evil has an end

items.comment: The end of the story is not an eternal conflict, but a world without tears, death or pain: "the former things have passed away". Evil is an episode, not the last word.

questions.text: What would it mean to you to have a life in which there is "no more" of the pain you experience today?

items.comment: Paul does not make light of suffering, but he weighs it: it is "not worth comparing" with the glory that is to be revealed. Present evil is real, but temporary.

questions.text: How does hope for a future that "outweighs" the present help you get through what is hard right now?

items.comment: The promise is strong: "affliction will not rise up a second time". God will resolve the problem of evil so thoroughly that it will never recur.

questions.text: Why does it matter that God will not only "stop" evil, but remove its source forever?

items.label: why evil will not return "a second time" (Nah 1:9)
items.content: Since evil once arose in a perfect world, a question follows: can it break out again? The answer of the great controversy is: no. God does not destroy evil immediately precisely in order to reveal its nature before the whole universe - so thoroughly that when the conflict ends, no one will ever want to repeat it. The universe is to be forever safe not through coercion, but through evidence.

application.text: Evil does not come from God and did not belong to his world. It arose where freedom - necessary for love to be genuine - was used against God, first in heaven, then on earth. We live in the middle of the great controversy, but not without hope: God is not the author of suffering, but the One who himself entered into it on the cross and promised a definitive end to evil. Your suffering is real - but it is not the last word.
application.challenge: Think of one specific instance of suffering (your own or that of someone close to you) that makes you ask "where is God?". Instead of laying it on God as the guilty one, bring it to God as your Ally in the battle - say it directly in prayer. Write down one sentence you would want to hear from God about it, and set it alongside the promise of Rev 21:4.
